strengths: Comprehensive and well-designed evaluation: experiments cover 48 VRP variants (roughly 3x more than prior multi-task works such as MT-POMO and MVMoE), plus out-of-distribution attribute settings (capacity, time windows, distance limits), large-scale CVRPLIB instances, and few-shot finetuning to unseen variants (Tables 1-2, 6-13). Consistent gains over recent neural baselines (~10% optimality-gap reduction in aggregate) strengthen the central claim.

The unified VRP environment (MDOVRPMBLTW with attribute toggles, detailed action-mask logic in Appendix A) is a genuinely useful contribution: it cleanly formalizes attribute composition, is well documented, and enables mixed batch training and easy extension to new variants. This infrastructure is valuable for future work regardless of model details.

The proposed techniques are sensible and each is ablated: Mixed Batch Training (per-batch variant mixing) and multi-task reward normalization (Section 4.3, Appendix D.4-D.5) are shown to improve stability and convergence, including under imbalanced variant distributions; the Efficient Adapter Layers (EAL) zero-initialization trick elegantly preserves zero-shot performance, outperforming the adapter approach of Lin et al. (2024) at step 0 and after finetuning (Table 2, D.7).

Good reproducibility: code is publicly available, hyperparameters are fully specified (Table 4), data generation procedures are described in detail (Appendix A.1), and baseline setups (solvers, time limits, augmentation, multistarts) are specified. Honest treatment of differences in training protocol relative to baselines (training on all variants rather than single-attribute restriction).

Thorough interpretability analysis (t-SNE across encoder layers and variants, Appendix D.6) provides evidence that Global Attribute Embeddings yield better-structured latent representations, supporting the design rationale rather than only reporting aggregate gaps.

Honest limitations discussion (Section 6, Appendix C.3-C.4): acknowledges remaining gaps to HGS/OR-Tools, the specialized nature of the model relative to 'generalist CO' ambitions, and possible future integration with local search/decomposition.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty at the component level: the encoder improvements (RMSNorm, pre-norm, SwiGLU, FlashAttention) are direct imports from modern LLM practice; EAL is a small modification of existing adapter approaches (zero-padding rows of Lin et al.'s AL); MBT is essentially reweighting batch composition; reward normalization is a standard baseline-scaling trick. The main contributions are system-level integration and thorough evaluation rather than new methods, which may limit the paper's conceptual impact.

The 'foundation model' framing is somewhat overclaimed: the model is small (128-dim, 6 layers), trained on a fixed set of 7 attributes over uniform synthetic distributions, and the term suggests capabilities (broad transfer, scaling behavior) that are not systematically demonstrated (no scaling-law-style experiments, no natural/clustered distributions in the main experiments).

Performance remains well behind classical OR solvers: HGS-PyVRP and OR-Tools dominate in nearly all cells of Table 1, so the practical significance of the gains is restricted to comparisons within the learning-based family; the paper discusses this but the practical deployment case is not yet established.

Some evidential gaps in the motivating claims: Figure 4's claim that non-MBT training 'leads to instability toward a single task' is more of an illustration than evidence, and the Appendix B text contains inconsistencies (Eq. 12 describes Instance Normalization while Section 4.2.1 claims RMSNorm; Eq. 13 mentions ReLU while the SwiGLU block is claimed), which undermine confidence in the presentation of the model details.

The ablation in Figure 5 uses MT-POMO as the reference point rather than an ablated RouteFinder without any proposed components, making the individual attribution of gains (Global Embeddings vs. MBT vs. reward normalization vs. encoder) less crisp than it could be; additionally, MBT changes both data distribution and gradient properties, so its isolated effect vs. reward normalization is entangled in the main results.

Novelty relative to the closest prior work (Liu et al., 2024a; Zhou et al., 2024) is incremental: the paper builds directly on their attribute-composition, POMO, and MoE machinery, and reviewers may view the contribution as an engineering refinement plus benchmark rather than a new research direction.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 48 VRP variants (3x more than prior work), with ablations for each proposed component (Fig. 5, App. D.3-D.6), out-of-distribution tests over capacity/time-window/duration-limit values (App. D.1), large-scale CVRPLIB evaluation (App. D.2), and zero-shot plus few-shot finetuning to unseen attributes (Sec. 5.3, App. D.7).

The unified VRP environment (MD-OVRPMBLTW with toggleable attributes) is a useful engineering contribution that cleanly supports attribute composition and future extension, and the environment/action-mask logic is documented in detail (App. A.2).

Efficient Adapter Layers (EAL) are a sensible, well-motivated improvement over adapter layers from Lin et al. (2024): zero-padding initialization preserves zero-shot performance while still enabling adaptation, and the ablation at 'step 0' convincingly isolates this effect (Table 2).

Strong reproducibility: code is publicly released, hyperparameters are fully specified (Table 4), data generation is precisely described (App. A.1), licenses of used assets are listed (Table 5), and limitations are honestly discussed (e.g., sub-par performance vs. HGS, in App. C.3).

Results consistently show improvements over recent multi-task baselines (MTPOMO, MVMoE) across nearly all settings, and the advantage grows out of distribution (Tables 6-8), which supports the foundation-model motivation.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The core ideas are combinations of existing techniques: attribute composition is taken from Liu et al. (2024)/Zhou et al. (2024), the RL training is POMO with a normalized baseline, Mixed Batch Training amounts to mixing tasks within a batch (a standard multi-task practice, here mostly re-enabling it), and reward normalization is a known family of techniques evaluated empirically rather than a new method. The encoder changes (RMSNorm, pre-norm, SwiGLU, FlashAttention) are imported wholesale from modern LLM practice. The paper is best viewed as careful systems/engineering work rather than a methodological advance.

The 'foundation model' framing is somewhat overclaimed. The model is a multi-task VRP solver over 7 predefined attributes with uniform synthetic instance generation; the finetuning experiments cover only two new attributes (MD, MB), and generalization to genuinely new constraint types (new attribute semantics, not just attribute on/off) is untested.

Substantial gap to classical OR solvers remains: HGS-PyVRP is roughly 2-4% better than the best learned model across most variants of Table 1, so the practical significance depends heavily on the speed/adaptability argument rather than solution quality.

Evaluation is mostly on uniform random synthetic instances up to n=100 in the main tables; the CVRPLIB results (App. D.2) still show ~12% average gaps, indicating limited real-world-scale validation of solution quality.

Some comparisons are potentially confounded: the authors retrain baselines under their own setup (differing from the original MTPOMO/MVMoE training regimes, as noted in Sec. 5), so part of the improvement may come from training-protocol differences rather than the proposed components, although the ablation studies partially mitigate this concern.

Mixed Batch Training's claimed stabilization benefit is shown mainly via loss curves and convergence plots (Figs. 9-11); a sharper quantitative characterization or analysis of why per-variant batching destabilizes training is missing.

strengths: Extensive and convincing empirical evaluation: 48 VRP variants (roughly 3x prior multi-task works), with consistent improvements over strong neural baselines (MTPOMO, MVMoE), plus out-of-distribution attribute generalization (Tables 6-8), large-scale CVRPLIB evaluation (Table 9), and three finetuning regimes for unseen attributes (Tables 10-13).

The unified VRP environment (MDOVRPMBLTW with attribute on/off composition) is a clean and reusable contribution that is well documented, including detailed data generation and action-mask logic in Appendix A, which supports reproducibility.

The proposed training techniques are sensible and empirically supported: Mixed Batch Training is shown via loss and validation-gap curves (Figures 9-11) to stabilize training, including under imbalanced variant distributions; multi-task reward normalization is ablated across four normalization schemes (Figure 8, D.4).

EAL (zero-padded augmented projection layers for finetuning to unseen attributes) is a simple but effective idea; Table 2 and Appendix D.7 show it preserves zero-shot performance and clearly outperforms the AL baseline of Lin et al. (2024).

Thorough ablation studies (Figure 5, D.3 encoder component ablations, D.4, D.5, D.6 t-SNE analyses) that isolate the contribution of each component, and an honest conclusion noting that generality comes at some cost to single-task solution quality and that neural solvers still trail traditional heuristics.

Good reproducibility: code publicly available, full hyperparameters (Table 4), hardware details, licenses of used assets, and the fair-for-comparison note that all models (including baselines) use FlashAttention.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate: the core framework (attribute composition for zero-shot VRP generalization) is built directly on Liu et al. (2024) and Zhou et al. (2024), and the architectural upgrades (pre-norm/RMSNorm, SwiGLU, FlashAttention) are imported from modern LLM practice rather than being VRP-specific insights. MBT and reward normalization are straightforward engineering; EAL is a small modification of existing adapter layers (zero-padding instead of re-initialization).

The 'foundation model' framing is somewhat overstated: coverage is limited to 7 attribute types and uniform 2D coordinate distributions; the paper acknowledges this in Appendix C.3 and the conclusion, but the term may inflate expectations relative to true foundation-model breadth.

Absolute solution quality remains far from strong traditional solvers: HGS-PyVRP dominates all neural methods on every variant (e.g., ~1.2-3% gaps at n=50 and much larger gaps, up to 12-30%, on CVRPLIB X instances), so the practical significance is mainly relative to other neural solvers.

Baseline comparability caveat: the paper's setup differs from MTPOMO/MVMoE training (all variants trained on simultaneously rather than single-attribute restriction), so part of the gain may stem from data/training mixture rather than the proposed architecture; the ablations partially address this but a direct apples-to-apples comparison is not fully isolated.

Evaluation uses only greedy rollouts with dihedral augmentation; no sampling or search-based inference (which prior work shows can substantially change rankings), and no statistical significance or variance reporting for the main test tables.

Minor presentation issues: Figure 4's illustration of MBT is schematic and not evidence-bearing; some notation density (e.g., reward normalization, Eq. 6) could be streamlined; a few claims (e.g., 'more than 10% improvement in optimality gaps') are aggregate and not broken down per variant in the main text.
